title: Improvised tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding
mechanism_check: Life-threatening bleeding: bright red spurting blood or steady heavy flow that direct pressure cannot slow.
A tourniquet works by compressing the artery against the bone above the wound — it must be tight enough to stop arterial flow.
Scene safety first: do not become a second casualty.
improvised_tools: A cravat: a shirt sleeve, bandana, or strip of cloth 3-4 inches wide (never wire, cord, or anything narrower than 2 inches).
A windlass: a sturdy stick, pen, or wrench to twist the cravat tight.
A watch or phone to note the time applied.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — shout for help, send someone to call emergency services.
Apply firm direct pressure with cloth while preparing the tourniquet.
Wrap the cravat 2-3 inches above the wound (never over a joint), tie a half-knot.
Place the windlass on the knot, tie a full knot over it, twist until bleeding stops.
Secure the windlass so it cannot unwind; note the time and tell responders.
Do NOT loosen or remove it once applied — that is for medical professionals.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not attempt if direct pressure controls the bleeding — pressure is always the first choice.
Do not attempt on neck, torso, or head wounds — tourniquets are for limbs only.
Do not use wire, rope, or narrow cord — they cut tissue instead of compressing arteries.

title: Improvised pressure dressing for severe bleeding
mechanism_check: Severe bleeding that may respond to pressure: steady dark-red flow from a wound you can reach and press on.
Pressure works by compressing damaged vessels against underlying tissue — it needs continuous, firm force.
If blood soaks through, the dressing stays on and more goes over it — never peel off a soaked dressing.
improvised_tools: The cleanest cloth available: shirts, towels, bandanas — pressure matters more than sterility in the moment.
A second cloth or wrap to bind the dressing in place; a belt or strip of clothing as a pressure band.
Your gloved or wrapped hands — avoid direct blood contact if you can.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — get emergency services coming before anything else.
Press the cloth directly onto the wound with the heel of your hand, hard.
If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top — do not remove the first layer.
Bind it tight with a wrap or belt to hold pressure while keeping the limb still.
Keep the injured person lying down and warm; keep talking to them.
Hand off to responders: tell them when it started and what you did.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not attempt if bleeding is spurting/arterial and pressure fails — escalate to a tourniquet (limbs) immediately.
Do not press on an object impaled in the wound — stabilize it in place and press around it.
Do not give the person food, drink, or aspirin.

title: Splint a fractured limb with found materials
mechanism_check: Suspected fracture: deformity, swelling, inability to bear weight, or a heard snap.
A splint immobilizes the joints above AND below the break — immobilizing only the break site lets it pivot.
Check circulation beyond the injury before and after splinting (warmth, color, pulse if you can find it).
improvised_tools: Rigid supports: sticks, trekking poles, rolled magazines, boards — longer than the injured segment.
Padding: clothing, towels, moss — between the rigid support and the limb.
Ties: bandanas, belts, torn strips — snug, never tourniquet-tight.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — a fracture needs medical evaluation.
Keep the limb as found; do not straighten a deformed fracture.
Pad the rigid supports and place them along the limb, spanning the joints above and below the break.
Tie snugly at several points — firm enough to immobilize, loose enough that fingers/toes stay warm and pink.
Recheck circulation after tying; loosen and re-tie if the extremity cools or numbs.
Keep the person still, warm, and lying down until help arrives.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not attempt to straighten, set, or 'pop back' any fracture or dislocation — you can sever vessels and nerves.
Do not attempt if the break may involve the spine, pelvis, or hip — immobilize in place and wait for professionals.
If toes/fingers go numb, pale, or cold after splinting: loosen immediately and re-tie.

title: Improvised stretcher and carries for evacuation
mechanism_check: Evacuation is needed when the person cannot walk and help cannot reach them.
The carry must not worsen the injury: spinal, pelvic, and hip injuries forbid most carries.
Test the stretcher with a healthy person or equivalent weight before loading the injured.
improvised_tools: Two sturdy poles (saplings, paddles, skis) + a blanket, tarp, or two jackets with sleeves threaded onto the poles.
Rope, belts, or cord to lash the fabric so it cannot slide.
Four to six bearers minimum for a loaded stretcher over rough ground.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — evacuation by litter is grueling and risky.
Rule out spinal injury: if suspected, do not move them — wait for professionals.
Build the litter: poles through jacket sleeves or fabric lashed between poles, test-loaded first.
Log-roll the person onto the litter keeping head, neck, and back aligned.
Bearers lift together on count; keep the litter level, injured person's head uphill.
Rest often; a dropped litter is worse than a slow carry.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not attempt any carry if spinal injury is suspected — moving them can cause paralysis.
Do not attempt if you lack enough bearers or the terrain risks a fall — a dropped patient is a second emergency.
If the person's condition worsens during the carry, stop, stabilize, and reassess.

title: Emergency shelter from cold and rain with what you carry
mechanism_check: Hypothermia kills: shivering stops being enough when core temperature drops — shelter is about stopping heat loss (wind, wet, ground).
The ground steals more heat than the air: insulation underneath matters as much as cover overhead.
Build small: a shelter you heat with your body must be just bigger than you.
improvised_tools: A trash bag or poncho as a vapor barrier; dry leaves, pine needles, or grass as insulation.
A ridgepole (fallen branch) + lean-to branches, or a simple debris hut.
Paracord, shoelaces, or vines for lashing.
steps: Call for help FIRST if you have any signal means — shelter buys time, rescue ends the emergency.
Pick high, dry ground out of the wind; avoid dry creek beds and lone tall trees.
Pile 6+ inches of dry insulation UNDER you before anything else.
Build the smallest windproof, waterproof cover you can fit in — trash-bag bivvy or debris hut.
Get out of wet clothes if you have anything dry; stuff insulation inside your clothing.
Stay put once sheltered unless you know exactly where safety is.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not attempt to walk out in deteriorating weather or darkness unless you know the route exactly.
Do not build a fire inside or against a debris shelter — carbon monoxide and ignition risk.
If someone stops shivering but is still cold and confused: severe hypothermia — handle gently, keep horizontal, get help.

title: Find water and make it safe when none is coming
mechanism_check: Dehydration impairs judgment before it threatens life — decide on water early, while you think clearly.
Clear running water is the best source; stagnant, discolored, or chemical-smelling water is the worst.
No field method makes chemical or heavy-metal contamination safe — source selection is the real purification.
improvised_tools: A cloth pre-filter + settling (let silt drop for 30 minutes, pour off the clear top).
A metal container and fire: a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 at altitude) kills pathogens.
Plain unscented bleach as backup: 2 drops per liter, wait 30 minutes (double if cloudy).
steps: Signal for help FIRST — water buys time, rescue ends the emergency.
Choose the clearest running source; avoid anything with chemical smell, sheen, or dead animals.
Pre-filter through cloth and let it settle; pour off the clear water.
Boil it rolling for 1 minute (3 above 6500 ft) — or bleach-dose and wait 30 minutes.
Ration by need: small steady sips; reduce exertion and sun exposure to slow loss.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not attempt to drink water with chemical contamination (fuel, pesticide, industrial smell) — no field method makes it safe.
Do not attempt seawater or urine — both worsen dehydration.
If someone is confused or stops sweating in heat: heat illness — shade, cool, and urgent help.

title: Signal for rescue with improvised means
mechanism_check: Rescuers find contrast, pattern, and repetition: three of anything is the universal distress signal.
Signal works only if someone can see or hear it — match the method to the terrain and time of day.
Stay near your last known position; moving makes you harder to find.
improvised_tools: A whistle (3 blasts, repeated) — carries farther than shouting and doesn't exhaust you.
A mirror, phone screen, or any shiny surface for flash signaling at aircraft.
Smoke by day (green vegetation on a fire), bright ground signals (X or SOS) in open areas.
steps: Stop moving and make yourself findable near your last known position.
Whistle: 3 blasts, pause, repeat — keep it going at intervals.
By day: build a smoky fire ready to light; lay out a large X or SOS in contrast material.
At aircraft sound: flash the mirror toward it in sweeps; wave bright cloth.
At night: fire, headlamp strobes, or phone light in groups of three.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST by any working means — signals are for when comms are dead.
Do not attempt to signal by leaving your shelter/position to climb exposed terrain in bad weather.
Do not start a signal fire you cannot control — a wildfire is a second emergency.

title: Treat for shock while waiting for help
mechanism_check: Shock: pale, cool, clammy skin; fast weak pulse; confusion or anxiety — the body failing to perfuse itself.
Shock follows bleeding, trauma, burns, severe illness — treat the cause AND the shock.
Warmth and stillness are the field treatments; everything else is for professionals.
improvised_tools: Coats, blankets, sleeping bags — insulation above and below the person.
Anything to elevate legs ~12 inches (pack, log) unless injury forbids it.
Calm talk — panic raises heart rate and worsens shock.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — shock is a medical emergency.
Control any bleeding first (pressure dressing / tourniquet for limbs).
Lay the person flat; elevate legs about 12 inches unless head, spine, or leg injury forbids.
Insulate above and below; keep them warm but do not overheat.
Talk calmly; monitor breathing and responsiveness until help arrives.
Tell responders everything: what happened, what you did, when.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not attempt if spinal injury is suspected — do not move them, keep them as found.
Do not give food, drink, or medication — aspiration and surgical risk.
If breathing stops or they become unresponsive: begin CPR if trained and continue until help takes over.

title: Size up an emergency scene before touching a patient
mechanism_check: Scene safety decides everything: traffic, fire, electricity, violence, and unstable structures kill rescuers who skip this step.
BSI first: gloves or improvised barriers before any contact with blood or fluids.
Size-up is information, not treatment: count patients, note mechanism of injury, decide what help to call for.
improvised_tools: A phone — or a bystander sent with your exact location and patient count — to call emergency services.
Gloves; without them, plastic bags or spare clothing layers as fluid barriers.
A flashlight or phone light to scan for hazards before entering the scene.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — get help moving toward you before touching anyone.
Stop at the edge of the scene: scan for hazards that could make you the second patient.
Barrier up against blood and fluids.
Count patients; check responsiveness with a shout and a shoulder tap — never shake.
Note what hurt them (fall, crash, crush): mechanism of injury predicts hidden injuries.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — size-up buys time for help; it never replaces it.
Do not attempt rescue if the scene is unsafe for you — a second victim helps no one.
Do not move patients during size-up except to stop immediate life threats or escape danger.

title: Sort multiple patients with START-style triage
mechanism_check: Triage sorts; it does not treat. When patients outnumber rescuers, sorting decides who gets the next pair of hands.
START checks three things in under a minute per patient: respirations, perfusion (pulse and major bleeding), mental status.
Categories are priorities, not diagnoses: immediate, delayed, minor (walking wounded), deceased/expectant.
improvised_tools: Tags or tape: mark each patient red/yellow/green/black — or write the category on tape on their forehead.
A watch or counted seconds for the breathing-rate check.
Helpers: direct the walking wounded to one marked spot so they stop consuming rescuer time.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — triage exists to aim arriving help, not replace it.
Send everyone who can walk to one marked spot: the walking wounded (minor/green) are sorted.
Check each remaining patient: breathing? If not, open the airway once — still not breathing means deceased/black; move on.
Breathing over 30 per minute goes immediate/red; check pulse and major bleeding — uncontrolled bleeding is immediate/red.
Can follow simple commands goes delayed/yellow; cannot follow commands goes immediate/red.
Re-triage when help arrives or conditions change — categories are never permanent.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — triage aims professional help; it never substitutes for it.
Do not attempt triage when a life threat is in front of you and you are alone — treat first, sort second.
Do not attempt anything beyond sorting and positioning — no advanced procedures; that is for professionals.
Do not move red patients to 'better' spots unless the spot itself is dangerous.

title: Emergency patient moves: drags and extrication when danger is immediate
mechanism_check: The spine rule: a patient with suspected spinal injury stays put unless the location itself will kill them — fire, collapse, traffic, water.
A drag moves the body as one unit along the ground; low, slow, and straight keeps the spine aligned.
Extrication is removal from danger, not transport: get clear first, proper carry second.
improvised_tools: Their clothing: a shirt or jacket gathered at the shoulders makes a drag handle.
A blanket, coat, or tarp slid under the patient for a blanket drag.
Your own body: a shoulder drag (patient's wrists over your shoulders) for short moves.
steps: Call for professional help FIRST — move only to escape immediate danger, never for convenience.
Decide: is the danger (fire, collapse, traffic) worse than the move? If not, do not move them.
Keep head, neck, and back in line — pull along the body's long axis.
Clothes drag: gather clothing behind the neck and shoulders, crouch low, lean back and drag.
Blanket drag: slide a blanket under them and pull from the head end.
Once clear of danger, stop moving them and treat in place until help arrives.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help FIRST — improvisation is last resort when no help or equipment is coming.
Do not move a patient with suspected spinal injury unless immediate danger forces it.
Do not attempt lifts or carries alone when a drag will do — dropped patients gain new injuries.
Do not drag farther than the danger zone — switch to a proper carry once clear.
